mn56:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Nālanda in Pavārika’s Mango Grove.
mn56:2.1: Now on that occasion the Nigaṇṭha (Jain) Nātaputta was staying at Nālanda with a large assembly of Nigaṇṭhas.
mn56:2.2: Then when the Nigaṇṭha Tall Ascetic (Dīgha Tapassi) had wandered for alms in Nālanda and had returned from his alms-round after the meal, he went to Pavārika’s Mango Grove to see the Blessed One, and exchanged greetings with him,
mn56:2.3: and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he stood at one side. When he had done so, the Blessed One said to him:
mn56:2.4: ‘There are seats, ascetic, sit down if you like.’
mn56:3.1: When this was said, the Tall Ascetic took a lower seat and sat down at one side.
mn56:3.2: When he had done so, the Blessed One asked him:
mn56:3.3: ‘Ascetic, how many kinds of kamma does the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta describe for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma?’
mn56:3.4: ‘Friend Gotama, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is not accustomed to use the description “kamma, kamma”;
mn56:3.5: the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is accustomed to use the description “rod, rod”.’
mn56:3.6: ‘Then, ascetic, how many kinds of rod does the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta describe for the performance of evil action, for the perpetration of evil action?’
mn56:3.7: ‘Friend Gotama, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta describes three kinds of rods for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma, that is to say:
mn56:3.8: the bodily rod, the verbal rod, and the mental rod.’
mn56:3.9: ‘How then, ascetic, is the bodily rod one, the verbal rod another, and mental rod another?’
mn56:3.10: ‘The bodily rod is one, friend Gotama, the verbal rod is another, and the mental rod is another.’
mn56:3.11: ‘Of these three kinds of rods, ascetic, thus analysed and distinguished, which kind of rod does the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta describe as the most reprehensible for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma: the bodily rod, or the verbal rod, or the mental rod?’
mn56:3.12: ‘Of these three kinds of rod, friend Gotama, thus analysed and distinguished, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta describes the bodily rod as the most reprehensible for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma, and not so much the verbal rod, or the mental rod.’
mn56:3.13: ‘Do you say the bodily rod, ascetic?’
mn56:3.14: ‘I say the bodily rod, friend Gotama.’
mn56:3.15: ‘Do you say the bodily rod, ascetic?’
mn56:3.16: ‘I say the bodily rod, friend Gotama.’
mn56:3.17: ‘Do you say the bodily rod, ascetic?’
mn56:3.18: ‘I say the bodily rod, friend Gotama.’
mn56:3.19: So the Blessed One made the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, maintain his statement up to the third time.
mn56:4.1: When this was said, the Tall Ascetic asked the Blessed One:
mn56:4.2: ‘Friend Gotama, how many kinds of rod do you describe for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma?’
mn56:4.3: ‘Ascetic, a Tathāgata is not accustomed to use the description “rod, rod”;
mn56:4.4: a Tathāgata is accustomed to use the description “kamma, kamma”.’
mn56:4.5: ‘But, friend Gotama, how many kinds of kamma do you describe for the performance of evil kammas, for the perpetration of evil kammas?’
mn56:4.6: ‘Ascetic, I describe three kinds of kammas for the performance of evil kammas, for the perpetration of evil kammas, that is to say:
mn56:4.7: bodily kamma, verbal kamma, and mental kamma.’
mn56:4.8: ‘How then, friend Gotama, is bodily kamma one, verbal kamma another, and mental kamma another?’
mn56:4.9: ‘Bodily kamma is one, ascetic, verbal kamma is another, and mental kamma is another.’
mn56:4.10: ‘Of these three kinds of kamma, friend Gotama, thus analyzed and distinguished, which kind of kamma do you describe as the most reprehensible for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma: bodily kamma or verbal kamma or mental kamma?’
mn56:4.11: ‘Of these three kinds of kamma, ascetic, thus analyzed and distinguished, I describe mental kamma as the most reprehensible for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma, and not so much bodily kamma or verbal kamma.’
mn56:4.12: ‘Do you say mental kamma, friend Gotama?’
mn56:4.14: ‘Do you say mental kamma, friend Gotama?’
mn56:4.16: ‘Do you say mental kamma, friend Gotama?’
mn56:4.18: So the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, made the Blessed One maintain his statement up to the third time, after which he rose from his seat and went to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.
mn56:5.1: Now on that occasion the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta was seated together with a very large assembly of laymen from Bālaka, most prominent among them being Upāli.
mn56:5.2: The Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta saw the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, coming;
mn56:5.3: and when he saw him he asked him:
mn56:5.4: ‘Now where are you coming from in broad day, Ascetic?’
mn56:5.5: ‘I have come from the monk Gotama’s presence, venerable sir.’
mn56:5.6: ‘Did you have some conversation with the monk Gotama, Ascetic?’
mn56:5.7: ‘I had some conversation with the monk Gotama, venerable sir.’
mn56:5.8: ‘How was your conversation with the monk Gotama, then, Ascetic?’
mn56:5.9: Then the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, related to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta all his conversation with the Blessed One.
mn56:6.1: When this was said the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta told him:
mn56:6.2: ‘Good, good, (on the part of the) Ascetic:
mn56:6.3: As by a well-taught disciple who knows his teacher’s Dispensation rightly, so it has been declared by the Tall Ascetic to the monk Gotama!
mn56:6.4: What does the trivial mental rod count in comparison with the gross bodily rod?
mn56:6.5: On the contrary, the bodily rod is the most reprehensible for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma, and not so much the verbal rod and the mental rod.’
mn56:7.1: When this was said, the householder Upāli said to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
mn56:7.2: Good, good, venerable sir, (on the part of) the Tall Ascetic:
mn56:7.3: As by a well-taught disciple who knows his teacher’s Dispensation rightly, so it has been declared by the venerable Ascetic to the monk Gotama:
mn56:7.4: “What does the trivial mental rod count for in comparison with the gross bodily rod?
mn56:7.5: On the contrary, the bodily rod is the most reprehensible for the performance of evil kamma for the perpetration of evil kamma, and not so much the verbal rod or the mental rod.”
mn56:7.6: Now, venerable sir, I shall go and prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong on the basis of this statement.
mn56:7.7: If the monk Gotama maintains to me as he has been made to maintain by the venerable Tall Ascetic, I shall drag the monk Gotama to and fro and round about with argument as a strong man might seize a long-haired ram by the hair and drag him to and fro and round about.
mn56:7.8: I will drag the monk Gotama to and fro and round about with argument as a strong brewer’s workman might throw a big brewer’s seive into a deep water tank, and taking it by the corners, drag it to and fro and round about.
mn56:7.9: I will shake the monk Gotama down and shake him up and thump him about with argument as a strong brewer’s mixer might take a strainer by the corners and shake it down and shake it up and thump it about.
mn56:7.10: And just as a sixty-year old elephant might go down into a pond and have great sport in the game of hemp-washing, so too, I shall have great sport, I fancy, in the game of hemp-washing the monk Gotama!
mn56:7.11: Venerable sir, I shall go and prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong on the basis of this statement.’
mn56:7.12: ‘Go, householder, and prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong on the basis of this statement;
mn56:7.13: for either I should prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong, or else the Tall Ascetic or you yourself.’
mn56:8.1: When this was said, the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, said to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
mn56:8.2: ‘Venerable sir, I should prefer that the householder Upāli did not (try to) prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong;
mn56:8.3: for the monk Gotama is a magician and he knows a converting magic by which he converts disciples of other sectarians.’
mn56:8.4: ‘It is impossible, ascetic, it cannot happen, that the householder Upāli should go over to the monk Gotama’s discipleship;
mn56:8.5: but it is possible, it can happen, that the monk Gotama should come over to the householder Upāli’s discipleship.
mn56:8.6: Go, householder, and prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong;
mn56:8.7: for either I should prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong or else the Tall Ascetic or you yourself.’
mn56:9.1: For the second time, the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, said to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta: ‘Venerable sir, I should prefer that the householder Upāli did not (try to) prove...’ ‘It is impossible, ascetic, it cannot happen...’
mn56:9.2: For the third time, the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, said to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
mn56:9.3: ‘Venerable sir, I should prefer that the householder Upāli did not (try to) prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong;
mn56:9.4: for the monk Gotama is a magician and he knows a converting magic by which he converts disciples of other sectarians.’
mn56:9.5: ‘It is impossible, ascetic, it cannot happen that the householder Upāli should go over to the monk Gotama’s discipleship...
mn56:9.8: else the Tall Ascetic or you yourself.’
mn56:9.9: ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ the householder Upāli replied, and he rose from his seat, and after paying homage to him, keeping him on his right, he left to go to the Blessed One in Pavārika’s Mango Grove, and there, after paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he asked the Blessed One:
mn56:9.10: ‘Venerable sir, did the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, come here?’
mn56:9.11: ‘The Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, came here, householder.’
mn56:9.12: ‘Venerable sir, did you have some conversation with him?’
mn56:9.13: ‘I had some conversation with him, householder.’
mn56:9.14: ‘How was your conversation with him, then, venerable sir?’
mn56:9.15: Then the Blessed One related to the householder Upāli all his conversation with the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic.
mn56:10.1: When this was said, the householder Upāli said to the Blessed One:
mn56:10.2: ‘Good, good, venerable sir, (on the part of) the Tall Ascetic:
mn56:10.3: as by a well-taught disciple who knows his teacher’s Dispensation rightly, so it has been declared by the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, to the Blessed One!
mn56:10.4: What does the trivial mental rod count for in comparison with the gross bodily rod?
mn56:10.5: On the contrary, the bodily rod is the most reprehensible for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma, and not so much the verbal rod or the mental rod.’
mn56:10.6: ‘Householder, if you will debate on the basis of truth, we might have some conversation about this.’
mn56:10.7: ‘I will debate on the basis of truth, venerable sir,
mn56:10.8: so let us have some conversation about this.’

mn56:15.1: ‘Venerable sir, I was satisfied and convinced by the Blessed One’s very first simile;
mn56:15.2: nevertheless I conceived (the thought of) opposing the Blessed One thus since I desired to hear the Blessed One’s varied answers to the question.
mn56:15.3: Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!
mn56:15.4: The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama, as though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, holding up a lamp in the darkness for those with eyes to see forms.
mn56:15.5: Venerable sir, I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha.
mn56:15.6: Let the Blessed One remember me as follower who has gone to him for refuge for life.’
mn56:16.1: ‘Think it over, householder; it is good for such well-known people as you are to think matters over.’
mn56:16.2: ‘Venerable sir, I am even more satisfied and convinced by the Blessed One’s telling me that,
mn56:16.3: for the other sectarians, on acquiring me as their disciple, would carry a banner all over Nālanda to the effect that
mn56:16.4: “the householder Upāli has come to our discipleship”.
mn56:16.5: But on the contrary, the Blessed One tells me:
mn56:16.6: “Think it over, householder; it is good for such well-known people as you are to think matters over.”
mn56:16.7: So for the second time, venerable sir, I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha.
mn56:16.8: Let the Blessed One remember me as a follower who has gone to him for refuge for life.’
mn56:17.1: ‘Householder, your family has long been one supporting the Nigaṇṭhas, and so may you conceive that alms should be given to them when they come.’
mn56:17.2: ‘Venerable sir, I am even more satisfied and convinced by the Blessed One’s telling me that.
mn56:17.3: Venerable sir, I have heard this: “The monk Gotama says thus:
mn56:17.4: ‘Gifts should be given only to me; gifts should not be given to others.
mn56:17.5: Gifts should be given only to my disciples; gifts should not be given to others’ disciples.
mn56:17.6: Only what is given to me is very fruitful; not what is given to others.
mn56:17.7: Only what is given to my disciples is very fruitful; not what is given to others’ disciples.’
mn56:17.8: But on the contrary, the Blessed One encourages me to give gifts to the Nigaṇṭhas.
mn56:17.9: Anyway we shall know the time for that, venerable sir.
mn56:17.10: So for the third time, venerable sir, I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha.
mn56:17.11: Let the Blessed One remember me as a follower who has gone to him for refuge for life.’
mn56:18.1: Then the Blessed One gave the householder Upāli progressive instruction, that is to say,
mn56:18.2: talk on giving, on virtue, on the heavens; he explained the danger, the degradation and the defilement in sensual desires, and the blessings in renunciation.
mn56:18.3: When he knew that the householder Upāli’s mind was ready, receptive, free from hindrance, elated and confident, he expounded to him the teaching peculiar to the Enlightened Ones:
mn56:18.4: Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
mn56:18.5: Just as a clean cloth with all marks removed would take dye evenly,
mn56:18.6: so too, while the householder Upāli sat there, the spotless immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in him:
mn56:18.7: ‘All that is subject to arising is subject to cessation.’
mn56:18.8: Then the householder Upāli saw and reached and knew and fathomed the Dhamma; he crossed beyond uncertainty, he had done with questioning, gained intrepidity, and became independent of others in the Teacher’s Dispensation, and then he said to the Blessed One:
mn56:18.9: ‘Now, venerable sir, we must go; for we are busy and have much to do.’
mn56:18.10: ‘Now is the time, householder, to do as you conceive fit.’
mn56:19.1: Then delighting in the Blessed One’s words and agreeing with them the householder Upāli rose from his seat, after paying homage to the Blessed One, keeping him on his right, he left to return to his own house. There he addressed the doorkeeper thus:
mn56:19.2: ‘Good doorkeeper, from today on I close my door to the Nigaṇṭhas and the Nigaṇṭhīs and I open my door to the Blessed One’s bhikkhus, bhikkhunis, laymen followers and laywomen followers.
mn56:19.3: If any Nigaṇṭha comes, then tell him thus:
mn56:19.5: from today on the householder Upāli has come over to the Discipleship of the monk Gotama.
mn56:19.6: He has closed his doors to the Nigaṇṭhas, and he has opened his doors to the Blessed One’s bhikkhus, bhikkhunis, laymen followers and laywomen followers.
mn56:19.7: Venerable sir, if you have need of alms, wait here; they will bring it to you here.’
mn56:20.1: The Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, heard:
mn56:20.2: ‘The householder Upāli, it seems, has gone over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama.’
mn56:20.3: Then he went to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and told him:
mn56:20.4: ‘Venerable sir, I have heard thus: “The householder Upāli, it seems, has gone over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama.”’
mn56:20.5: ‘It is impossible, Ascetic, it cannot happen, that the householder Upāli should go over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama;
mn56:20.6: but it is possible, it can happen, that the monk Gotama might come over to the discipleship of the householder Upāli.’
mn56:20.7: A second time the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, told the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta: ‘Venerable sir, I have heard thus …’
mn56:20.8: A third time the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, told the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta …
mn56:20.11: ‘It is impossible, Ascetic, it cannot happen …’
mn56:20.12: ‘Venerable sir, shall I go and find out whether he has gone over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama or not?’
mn56:20.13: ‘Go, Ascetic, and find out whether he has gone over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama or not.’
mn56:21.1: Then the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, went to the householder Upāli’s house.
mn56:21.3: When he saw him, he told him:
mn56:21.5: from today on the householder Upāli has come over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama.
mn56:21.6: He has closed his doors to the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhis, and he has opened his doors to the Blessed One’s bhikkhus, bhikkhunis, laymen followers and laywomen followers.
mn56:21.7: Venerable sir, if you have need of alms, wait here; they will bring it to you here.’
mn56:21.8: ‘I have no need of alms, friend,’ he said, and he turned back and went to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and told him:
mn56:21.9: ‘Venerable sir, it is only too true. The householder Upāli has gone over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama.

mn56:23.8: Then the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta went with the large assembly of Niganthas to the hall of the central door.
mn56:24.1: Then whereas the householder Upāli had been used,
mn56:24.2: when he saw the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta coming in the distance, to go out to meet him and then after dusting with an upper robe the highest and best, chief and most superior seat of all there, seat him on it arranging the upper robe round him, he now being himself seated on the highest and best, chief and most superior seat, then told Nigaṇṭha Nātautta: ‘Venerable sir, there are seats; sit down if you wish.’
mn56:24.3: Then whereas the householder Upāli had been used, when he saw the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta coming in the distance, to go out to meet him and then after dusting with an upper robe the highest and best, chief and most superior seat of all there, seat him on it arranging the upper robe round him, he now being himself seated on the highest and best, chief and most superior seat, then told Nigaṇṭha Nātautta:
mn56:25.1: When this was said, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said:
mn56:25.2: ‘Householder, you are mad, you are imbecile;
mn56:25.3: you go (saying): “Venerable sir, I shall prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong” and you come back all caught up in a vast net of theory.
mn56:25.4: Just as if a man went to castrate someone and came back castrated on both sides, as if a man went to put someone’s eyes out and came back with both his eyes put out;
mn56:25.5: so you too, householder, go (saying): “Venerable sir, I shall prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong” and you come back all caught up in a vast net of theory.
mn56:25.6: Householder, you have been converted by the monk Gotama with his converting magic!’
mn56:26.1: ‘It is an auspicious converting magic, venerable sir,
mn56:26.3: Venerable sir, were my beloved relatives and kin converted by this conversion, it would be long for their welfare and happiness.
mn56:26.4: Were all those in the warrior-noble caste … the divine caste … the burgher caste … the artisan caste to be converted by this conversion, it would be long for their welfare and happiness.
mn56:26.5: Were the world with its gods, its Māras, and its (Brahma) Divinities, this generation with its monks and divines, with its kings and its men, to be converted by this conversion, it would be long for its welfare and happiness.
mn56:26.6: As to which, venerable sir, I shall give you a simile;
mn56:26.7: for some wise men understand by means of a simile the meaning of what is said.
mn56:27.1: ‘Venerable sir, there was once a divine who was old, aged and burdened with years, and his wife who was a young divine-caste girl was pregnant and near her confinement.
mn56:27.3: “Go, divine, and buy a young monkey in the market and bring it back to me as a playmate for my child.”
mn56:27.4: When this was said, he replied:
mn56:27.5: “Wait, madam, till you have borne the child;
mn56:27.6: if you bear a boy, then I will go the market and buy a young male monkey and bring it back to you as a playmate for your child;
mn56:27.7: but if you bear a girl, then I will go to the market and buy a young female monkey and bring it back to you as a playmate for your child.”
mn56:27.8: For the second time she made the same request and received the same answer.
mn56:27.9: For the third time she made the same request.
mn56:27.11: Then since he was in love with her and his mind bound, he went to the market and bought a young male monkey and brought it back, and he told her:
mn56:27.12: “I have bought a young male monkey in the market and brought it back to you as a playmate for your child.”
mn56:27.14: “Go, divine, take this young male monkey to Dyed-hand the dyer’s son and tell him:
mn56:27.15: “Good Dyed-hand, I want this young male monkey dyed the colour called ‘yellow-unguent’ and pounded and re-pounded and ironed on both sides.”
mn56:27.16: Then, since he was in love with her and his mind bound, he took the young male monkey to Dyed-hand the dyer’s son and told him:
mn56:27.17: “Good Dyed-hand, I want this young male monkey dyed the colour called ‘yellow-unguent’ and pounded and re-pounded and ironed on both sides.”
mn56:27.18: When this was said, Dyed-hand the dyer’s son told him:
mn56:27.19: “Venerable sir, this young male monkey of yours will suffer a dyeing but not a pounding or an ironing.”
mn56:27.20: So too, venerable sir, the theory of the foolish Nigaṇṭhas will suffer fools’ dyeing (with their delight in it) but not wise men’s; but it will not suffer testing or ironing out.”
mn56:27.21: And then, venerable sir, on another occasion that divine took a pair of new garments to Dyed-hand the dyer’s son and told him:
mn56:27.22: “Good Dyed-hand, I want this pair of new garments dyed the colour called ‘yellow-unguent’ and pounded and re-pounded and ironed on both sides.”
mn56:27.23: When this was said, Dyed-hand the dyer’s son told him:
mn56:27.24: “Venerable sir, this pair of new garments of yours will suffer dyeing and it will suffer a pounding and an ironing.”
mn56:27.25: So too, venerable sir, the theory of that Blessed One, Arahant and Fully Enlightened, will suffer wise men’s dyeing (with their delight in it), not fools’, and it will suffer both testing and ironing out.’
mn56:28.1: ‘Householder, the Assembly and the King know you thus:
mn56:28.2: “The householder Upāli is a disciple of the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.”
mn56:29.1: When this was said, the householder Upāli rose from his seat, and arranging his upper robe on one shoulder, he extended his hands palms together towards where the Blessed One was, and he told the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
mn56:29.2: ‘In that case, venerable sir, hear whose disciple I am:
mn56:29.3: There is Wise One who has cast off delusion,
mn56:29.4: his heart’s wildernesses abandoned, his victors vanquished,
mn56:29.5: He knows no anguish, he is quite even-minded,
mn56:29.6: mature in virtue, with true understanding;
mn56:29.7: He is beyond temptation, and he is stainless:
mn56:29.8: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.
mn56:29.9: He has done with questioning, abiding contented,
mn56:29.10: he spurns what is worldly, the vessel of gladness;
mn56:29.11: He has done the monk’s duty, his birth was human,
mn56:29.12: he bears his last body in a male existence;
mn56:29.13: He is utterly peerless, utterly spotless:
mn56:29.14: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.
mn56:29.15: He is undoubting, he is the most skilful,
mn56:29.16: as the Discipliner, the Excellent Leader;
mn56:29.17: He has none to surpass his dhammas all pure,
mn56:29.18: with no hesitation, he is the Revealer;
mn56:29.19: Conceit he has severed, he is the Hero:
mn56:29.20: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.
mn56:29.21: He leads the herds’ leaders, he cannot be measured,
mn56:29.22: his depths are unfathomed, attained to the Silence;
mn56:29.23: Provider of safety, possessor of knowledge,
mn56:29.24: in the True Dhamma standing, restrained in himself;
mn56:29.25: He has overcome passion, he is liberated:
mn56:29.26: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.
mn56:29.27: The Immaculate Tusker, who lives in remoteness
mn56:29.28: with fetters all shattered, and liberated;
mn56:29.29: He charms in discussion, is invested with wisdom,
mn56:29.30: his banner is lowered, he knows no more lusting;
mn56:29.31: He has done his subduing, has no diversifying:
mn56:29.32: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.
mn56:29.33: Of Sages the Seventh, with no schemes for deceiving
mn56:29.34: with the triple True Knowledge, attained to Divineness
mn56:29.35: He has done the Ablution, a master of oration
mn56:29.36: he knows tranquillization, as the Finder of Knowledge
mn56:29.37: He is first of all givers, and he is able:
mn56:29.38: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.
mn56:29.39: He is Noble, and he is self-developed
mn56:29.40: he has gained his objective, he is the Expounder,
mn56:29.41: He is mindful, and endowed with insight
mn56:29.42: and he is impartial, and unfastidious;
mn56:29.43: With no perturbation, of mastery Master:
mn56:29.44: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.
mn56:29.45: He has fared rightly, and practised meditation,
mn56:29.47: He is independent, and altogether fearless,
mn56:29.49: He has crossed over, and he shows us the crossing:
mn56:29.50: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.
mn56:29.51: Of surpassing serenity, with wide understanding,
mn56:29.52: with great understanding, he has done with all lusting;
mn56:29.53: A Tathāgata Perfect, the Sugata, Well-gone,
mn56:29.54: the Person Unrivalled, and likewise Unequalled;
mn56:29.55: He is intrepid, (supreme in all) talents:
mn56:29.56: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.
mn56:29.57: His craving is severed, he is enlightened,
mn56:29.58: and cleared of all clouding, completely untainted;
mn56:29.59: To him gifts can be given, most mighty of spirits,
mn56:29.61: The greatest in grandeur, he has climbed to fame’s summits:
mn56:29.62: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.
mn56:30.1: ‘When did you concoct that hymn of praise to the monk Gotama, householder?’
mn56:30.2: ‘Venerable sir, suppose there were a great heap of many kinds of flowers, and then a clever garland-maker or garland-maker’s apprentice knotted them into a multi-coloured garland,
mn56:30.3: so too, venerable sir, the Blessed One has many a praiseworthy quality, many hundred praise-worthy qualities.
mn56:30.4: Who would not praise the praiseworthy?’
mn56:31.1: Then since the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta was unable to bear this honour done to the Blessed One, hot blood gushed then and there from his mouth.
